boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Cool Spring record (July 17-18, 1864) in Early's Raid and Operations Against the B&O Railroad [June-August 1864]. The July 16 capture of Early's wagons near Purcellville, the July 19 fight at Ashby's Gap and the July 20 crossing are context. Campaign-wide marches, levies, captures, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen and live force fields read 13,000 total (US 5,000; CS 8,000); the source basis is not given. Pond says Wright had about 10,000 effective of the Sixth Corps and 650 of the Nineteenth on July 13, that Sullivan's and Mulligan's divisions were 7,000 strong and Duffie's cavalry 2,000, and that Crook brought two brigades 3,400 strong; he says about 1,000 dismounted cavalry stood beyond Thoburn's right. Crook says he sent three brigades under Thoburn across the river. Pond says Breckinridge attacked with his two divisions and Rodes with his; no Confederate count is given.
claims.rationale: The Union figures are command strengths on different days before the crossing, not the force engaged; the imported 5,000 and 8,000 are unvalidated. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Crook says Thoburn crossed about a mile and a half below the ford the enemy held. Pond places the crossing at Island Ford, where a Confederate picket fired from behind bushes until Wells's brigade found a wading-place a few hundred yards below, and says the retreat was across a river under fire from the bank. NPS says Thoburn made a stand behind a stone wall at the river's edge.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested report, a history and a summary; no map verification.

claims.value: Crook says Wright ordered him forward to Snickersville and Snicker's Ford, that the Sixth Corps was ordered up to support Thoburn, and that when Ricketts, commanding the corps, thought it imprudent to cross, he ordered Thoburn to fall back. Pond says Breckinridge attacked Thoburn's left and centre while Early sent Rodes against the right. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Early and Major General Horatio Wright; the live page gives Early as Major General.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report and a history; neither listed commander receives automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Confederate victory and the live result Confederate Victory. Crook says the assaults were repulsed and the remaining troops fell back in good order, the enemy not following until after dark; Pond says Thoburn's right was driven into the stream while the left withdrew in good order. NPS says the Union pursuit was delayed several days; Early retreated on the night of the 19th.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live casualty fields read 819 total (US 422; CS 397). Crook and Pond give Thoburn's loss as 65 killed, 301 wounded and 56 missing, total 422. Crook says he had no correct means of ascertaining the enemy's loss; no inspected passage gives the Confederate 397. Pond gives Duffie's loss at Snicker's Gap on the 17th as 17.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The Confederate figure's basis is not established.

open_questions: Wright's July 11-28 dispatches (read, not selected; the July 21 dispatch puts Snicker's Ferry losses at not over 200), Thoburn's, Wells's and Ely's reports and the Confederate division reports remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office and field despatches; it quotes the reports of the commanders it describes and is not independent of them. Crook's July 27 and October 12, 1864 reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVII, Part 1, are one family of interested Union accounts; Pond quotes them. The Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
